en: The *New Verses on the Various Patriarchs* by Qianfo of Quanzhou ends here.
The monk Huiguan of Zhongnan Shan composed the preface, and Master Tai of Nanyue authored the five hymns and ten verses. At that time, these were celebrated as a source of great renown. Furthermore—
Yuepu and Xiangyan were particularly adept at composing eulogies;
these are merely the beginnings of that which aids the Path.
From the successive entrustment of the Patriarchs' lamp, beginning with Kāśyapa and ending with Caoxi, [this lineage has been maintained].
Regarding the fact that, after the robe of faith of the thirty-third patriarch, it was passed on to only a few more individuals—
a matter not praised by the former sages— I, being both ignorant and afflicted by illness, find this to be a source of concern.
Although the *Baolin Zhuan* recounts these matters such that one may rely upon them after reading it, alas,
how can those who have forgotten their artifice yet remain indolent disparage its profound significance? That the late autumn is worthy of appreciation— how could they fail to see it?
The fool [Yuan] previously requested that Chan Master Qianfodeng Hanyang compose this, but he did not grant it;

yet before even a night had passed, the work was completed. As for the words and principles produced by Qianfo’s brush, the extraordinary phrases from the contemporary dialogues have perhaps been intermingled therein.
Although the characters therein are not numerous, the works of the various sages are all contained within them.
This is just like placing Mount Sumeru inside a mustard seed; the principle is one and the same.
For this reason, I have inscribed this upon paper and dipped my brush to compose this preface.
It was recorded by the Great Master Qingmingjue of the Later Tang, following the twenty-eight patriarchs of the Western Land and the six patriarchs of the land of Tang.
How great is Kāśyapa! He has secretly transmitted the Buddha’s mind. His body relies upon but a single robe, yet his speech is as deep as the ocean.
His deportment is dignified and orderly; his transformative teachings are profound and far-reaching.
Until we meet Maitreya, he shall remain steadfast at Mount Kukkuṭapāda.
The one of great learning, Ānanda, who raised high the banner of the Dharma;
He transmitted the Buddha’s golden verses and continued the silver lamp of the patriarchs. Foremost in compassion, peerless in wisdom, a successor to Kāśyapa;
Like the moon reflected upon the autumn river.
Venerable Garbha-vastra, a bright lamp in a dark room, the eyes and ears of humans and devas, the limbs of the Buddha-dharma;
neither mind nor form, without decrease and without increase—how excellent is this ultimate truth!
A great garuḍa in the ocean of awakening.
Upagupta: He eloquently poured forth the profound river; The mountain of Dharma was towering, and the tree of the Way spread its branches.
Counting-sticks filled his stone chamber; His corpse bound the celestial Māra.
His nature was not seventeen-fold; Awakening occurred in a single kṣaṇa.
The Great Being Togha renounced the world through non-self; he thoroughly understood the faculties and mastered the objects, like the hare-mark on the moon or a flower in the sky.
His essence is not a physical form; his principle issues from his very teeth to benefit beings according to their needs.

How could there be a *bāgua* (a type of gourd)? [The character for "gourd" is read as] *jiāo* (反) and can be used for drinking; the word for "melon" (*guā*) is also pronounced *báo*, meaning hailstone—thus it is a "hail-melon."
Mijia Zu was a seer who had mastered the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Having encountered the Master’s True Dharma, he observed that his own mind was biased;

though he had attained awakening, it was as if he had not yet awakened. His profound mysteries within mysteries led him to demonstrate the extinction of his supernormal powers, leaving the eight classes of beings in silent awe.
The Patriarch Vasumitra entered Mi-chê-shih. In delusion and awakening, the source is as such;
things and self are darkly one. Holding his wine vessel level, he carried it upon his neck.
The Buddha asked: "What is right and what is wrong? Who gains and who loses?"
Buddha Nandi, who greatly transformed the deluded masses; his mind was free from external dharmas, abiding in the high station of ultimate principle.
A general of the treatises in the Five Indias, a cloud-ladder for the three realms, he stood out with his sublime true spirit throughout the north, south, east, and west.
Vimalamitra: A great vessel perfected late; for fifty years he did not speak, and for fifty years he did not walk.
I encountered this man of realization, who suddenly accords with the state of non-arising;
like a cliff pine, he possesses steadfast integrity, and like an autumn fowl, he knows no fixed course.
The Great Venerable Ānanda, Enmeshed in the net of love and hatred, His measure equal to empty space, his path as refined as a flute;
His true essence is spontaneous, Relying on the truth to unfold through the youth of this world’s vast expanse;
The wild horse of the mind gallops on.
Pūrṇayaśas, your wisdom is like Mount Sumeru; your mind points toward the Dharma abiding beyond the body’s prosperity and decline.
Whether light or dark, hidden or manifest, seeing, hearing, the subtle and the profound—all are present before you, firmly established, never again to deviate.
The Venerable Aśvaghoṣa transformed flowers into a palace; the mists of Māra’s realm were rolled away and the winds of the Nandana Grove grew pure.
I wish to know the Buddha, yet I do not recognize those who are his companions.
Is it not that profound understanding is hidden? When a foot moves, dust arises.
Vīra, the Honored Sage, while on the path of practice, was a Mara-king; relying on his teacher’s instruction, he slew [the demon] to realize the True and Constant.
Why act so foolishly? Who is the one of long-standing virtue, whose fragrance is pure and whose nature is pristine—like orchids and sweet flags amidst frost and ice?
The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna transformed the dragon into mist; his mind, awakening to the Buddha-mind, abides yet does not abide.
His body manifests perfect realization, and the flow of Dharma falls like drenching rain.
When Deva’s faculties were thus engaged, who could fathom the dark intent?
Kāṇadeva’s virtue rises ever higher; Like a revolving fragrant elephant, he yawns with golden hair.
His spiritual resonance is like thunder from a cliff; His eloquence pours forth like autumnal waves.
From beginning to end, he is free from fixed realization; Do not mistake him for the King’s executioner.
Rāhu’s Way and Virtue—how could it be discussed with the mouth? It is only through the teacher’s explanation that one finds the gateway to humanity.
Holding the sun high, he brings clarity; his great illumination encompasses heaven and earth.
Without grasping or rejecting, he transmits this to his descendants.
Saṃghanandi, the Prince Zhuangyan, traveled nine layers of barriers and entered the mountains for a thousand li.
Regarding the metaphors of meditative concentration and the analogy of refined gold, his interpretations diverged from the beginning to the end, and his reasoning was stymied by his teacher;
suddenly, he exhausted [the limits of] his own [understanding].
Kāśyapa, who from youth understood the Buddha’s subtle intent, Held a precious mirror in his hand before the teacher Nandika;
Internally and externally free from obscurations, with eyebrows and eyes unimpaired—
The sound of the wind-blown bell, who else but I?
Kumārajīva constantly dwelt beneath the eaves; Having received the teacher’s grace, he served his father without weariness.
By nature not one for tempering, he would not deign to rely on hammers or tongs;
Sitting alone upon a single mat, he was venerated by humans and devas alike.
Śāṇakavāsin: His bearing was lofty and his appearance ancient; his staff had six rings and his field not half a mu.
Under his words, nothing was not born; where could he not universally extend his hand?
He entered the marketplace, whether in other lands or this soil.
Vasubandhu, though practicing by not lying down, despite his diligent exertion, ended up becoming indolent.
Because of seeing through the finger, he saw the finger itself; encountering songs and clapping, he joined in the harmony, yet all was like bubbles and illusions—without reality.
To listen to one's emotions is no more than a transgression.
Discerning the stupa, subduing the valiant; the Prince of Sovereignty, thundering so that the hibernating move and the false teachers lose their teeth.
With divine power and the six supernormal faculties, the fragrance of the Way reaches for a thousand *li*;
since sound and form are eternally true, what need is there for deaf ears?
Venerable Hekle, whose supreme virtue is unattainable, Who speaks with extraordinary brilliance according to his natural spontaneity,
Whose merit surpasses the two benefits, And whose fame is such that the myriad nations bow their heads in refuge—
To you, the Patriarch Lin-dan-pu, we pay homage.
Venerable Siṃha, praised and revered by humans and devas; In the void, he spreads his wings like a crane soaring between blue clouds.
As soon as the drum of debate sounds, he drives the wheel of Dharma aloft, Crushing the ranks of heterodox followers and revealing the true place of departure.
Vasubandhu has long been free from clinging; until he meets the Author, he will never hear the Fist.
He transmits the Master’s robe and bowl; as a bridge and boat for saving beings, his wondrous vision lies within the heart—how could it depend on words?
Not inferior to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it surpasses the King’s celebration of his birthday.
High and remote as the consort of space, it ascends toward the practice of the Way; it is the pillar and beam of the Buddha-Dharma.
The King regards it with reverence, penetrating its essence as if examining it under a lens—the golden mirror of the Patriarchs’ Hall.
Prajñātāra—whose childhood name was Yaṣṭikā—lost both parents and wandered east and west.
One morning he realized the hair of a tortoise; he constantly lamented the drying of the waters, yet his fruit was full of Bodhi.
The source of the Way is vast and remote.
Bodhidharma transformed through the Way in non-action; for nine years at Shaoshi, he was the patriarch of the Six Schools.
He manifested his passing at Neng’er, returning to the West with his single shoe.
The Liang Heaven offered no memorial, yet Huike transmitted the robe.
The Second Patriarch was a man of profound learning; his conduct was firm and resolute.

His mind penetrated the Three Vehicles, while his spirit rested upon the Five Peaks. A *qilin* among those in heaven, a *yuezhuo* among those in the human realm, he severed his arm to manifest his spiritual resolve, remaining pure and untainted amidst the world.
The Great Master, the Third Patriarch, true son of all kings: his words emerge from the profound and subtle, his mind free of "this" or "that.
At times he dwells among mountain forests; at times he resides in the marketplace.
He manifests the flowers of the ground of practice, fragrant with the scent of sandalwood.
The Four Patriarchs, fourteen [generations]. Because the Master attained liberation, though his path was solitary while in the world, his compassion and measure were vast;
he forever severed the flickering [of delusion]. From the beginning to the end of the sublime Dharma, the fruit was few and the flowers many; he endured to transmit the robe and bowl.
The Fifth Patriarch at seven years of age, Thoroughly penetrating that which lies beyond words: The stone ox breathes mist, the wooden horse swallows the air;
Body and mind are eternally quiescent, Principle and phenomena both profoundly mysterious.
Without emotion, without seed— A thousand years, ten thousand years.
The Master went to Huangmei; having received the essential meaning, he came south.
Thereupon, through the principle of the banner, the thunder of the Dharma shook the world. Dao Ming met with misfortune, and Shen Xiu encountered a turning back.
Although the robe was not transmitted, the flowers of the Way bloomed throughout the land.
Master Guanyin, whose name was Huairang, took Prajñā as his refuge and served as a master craftsman in the gate of Chan.
His virtue was lofty as the Five Peaks, and his mental capacity encompassed the Four Oceans.
He had six dharma heirs, among whom Mazu rose to prominence like a sovereign king.
The True Person of Jishui appeared in the world at Luling; he alone upheld a single lineage that transcends the Three Vehicles.
Like the moon illuminating from within the waves, he walked upon water amidst the flames.
He revealed the wondrous assembly of the Lord, expounding upon the correspondence between the robe and the contemplation.
The National Teacher of the Tang Dynasty widely disseminated the great legacy: exploring the moon at Caoxi and boarding a boat on the Wei River.
When the Two Heavens questioned him, the fourfold assembly cast aside their equal talents;
his brilliance was so supreme that even Great-Ear felt ashamed.
Nanyue Shitou: The waters of Ji divide and flow; The hermitage rests in emerald caves, drawn by white oxen.
Having perfected his learning like the horn of a qilin, His fame spreads like a divine ship.
A monk asked about the Pure Land: If there is no defilement, what is there to seek?
Master of Horses, Dao-i: his practice is entirely of the eternal metal and stone. Having awakened to the root, he transcends;
seeking the branches is but weary toil. Long since his body and mind were settled, he cast them all away at once.
In the great transformation of Nanchang, the cold pines stand a thousand feet tall.
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Daozhen of Sanjie Temple in Shazhou.
